papers.title: Field-level modeling of halo and galaxy alignments
papers.authors: Nickolas Kokron, Mikhail M. Ivanov, James M. Sullivan
papers.abstract: We develop an effective field theory (EFT) of intrinsic alignments at the level of spin-2 field fluctuations of large-scale structure tracers, such as the shapes of galaxies and dark matter halos. Our perturbative model includes the non-linear treatment of the Zel'dovich displacement, and contains all necessary shape operators through the third order. We apply our field-level model to the full 3D distribution of galaxy shapes, whose sky projections are a known contaminant of cosmic shear measurements. Our field-level EFT model achieves a better description of the helicity fields of dark matter halo shapes than the standard non-linear alignment (NLA) and tidal torquing + tidal alignment (TATT) models in the literature, as evidenced by improved correlations with the simulations' initial conditions. We perform precision measurements of field-level bias parameters by means of a generalized least-squares problem, for which we derive an optimal estimator and analytic covariance matrices. We measure the full set of linear, quadratic, and cubic shape bias coefficients as a function of halo mass in the $\texttt{Quijote}$ N-body simulations. We then study the intrinsic alignments of galaxies in the $\texttt{FLAMINGO}$ hydrodynamical simulation, focusing on observationally relevant samples: spirals, ellipticals, luminous red galaxies (LRG) and emission-line galaxies (ELG). We detect linear and nonlinear alignment coefficients at high significance for LRG, spiral and elliptical galaxies. We also find evidence for non-zero density-weighted tidal bias coefficient of the simulated ELG. This work supports the notion that EFT-based models of alignments will be paramount in optimally extracting constraints from future shape correlations, and lays the foundation for the development of simulation-based priors for future galaxy shape samples.

They prove that a theoretical redundancy reduces the independent third-order shape basis from 11 to 10 operators, and construct an optimal generalized least-squares (GLS) estimator with analytic covariance matrices to extract shape bias parameters without cosmic variance. Applying their estimator to dark matter halos in Quijote and hydrodynamical galaxy samples in FLAMINGO, they show that the field-level EFT describes shape helicity fields significantly better than NLA or TATT and enables direct calibration of linear and non-linear alignment priors for weak lensing analyses.

papers.title: Two-dimensional galaxy cluster shapes using lensing data: a simulated analysis
papers.authors: C. Giocoli, M. Meneghetti, G. Despali, L. Moscardini, E. Rasia, G. Lesci, W. Cui, G. Yepes
papers.abstract: Context. Cluster morphology reflects assembly history and dynamical state. High-resolution weak lensing can reveal departures from spherical symmetry, but its ability to recover two-dimensional shapes remains less explored. Aims. We assess how reliably weak lensing recovers projected cluster morphology and its dependence on orientation and dynamical state. We also compare large-scale weak-lensing morphology with that traced by strong lensing near the cluster centre. Methods. We study three clusters at $z=0.22$ from The Three Hundred Project, representing relaxed, mildly disturbed and unrelaxed systems. For each, we consider three random projections and three along the principal axes of the mass tensor. For each projection, we generate 128 weak-lensing catalogues with a source density of 30 arcmin$^{-2}$ and intrinsic ellipticity dispersion $\sigma_{\epsilon}=0.3$. We constrain mass and concentration from one-dimensional NFW and BMO fits, then recover ellipticity, position angle and centre using a two-dimensional elliptical NFW model. We also measure morphology from true convergence maps, Kaiser \& Squires reconstructions and strong-lensing tangential critical lines. Results. Recovered parameters depend on orientation and dynamical state. The relaxed cluster has similar inner and large-scale shapes, whereas disturbed systems appear more elliptical centrally. Two-dimensional weak-lensing modelling recovers the projected mass orientation despite source sampling and shape noise. Kaiser \& Squires reconstructions recover the position angle well but favour rounder mass distributions. Centroid offsets are larger in unrelaxed systems. Conclusions. Combining weak- and strong-lensing morphology probes cluster structure across physical scales and offers a promising way to investigate morphology and dynamical state.

The authors analyze hydrodynamical zoom simulations of three galaxy clusters at $z=0.22$ from The Three Hundred Project (spanning relaxed, mildly disturbed, and unrelaxed states) viewed along six lines of sight, generating mock weak lensing catalogs and strong lensing maps. By fitting 2D elliptical NFW profiles and performing Kaiser-Squires mass reconstructions, they test how accurately full 2D lensing can recover cluster ellipticity, orientation, and centroid offsets across physical scales.

papers.title: Does the Escape Fraction Prescription Shape Reionization History and Morphology?
papers.authors: Pulkit Sheoran, Ankita Bera, Sultan Hassan
papers.abstract: The escape fraction of ionizing photons, $f_{\rm esc}$, is one of the least constrained quantities of the Epoch of Reionization (EoR), and the opacity of the intergalactic medium prevents its direct measurement at high redshifts. We constrain three power-law parameterizations, $f_{\rm esc}(z)$, $f_{\rm esc}(M_{\rm h})$, and $f_{\rm esc}(z, M_{\rm h})$, against JWST UV luminosity functions and EoR observables (the ionizing emissivity, the neutral hydrogen fraction, and the Thomson optical depth) using Markov Chain Monte Carlo, with priors that allow $f_{\rm esc}$ to either increase or decrease with redshift and halo mass. We then propagate the best-fit models into the semi-numerical simulation SimFast21 and compare their ionization morphology and 21 cm power spectra with those of a constant-$f_{\rm esc}$ model. All models reproduce the observations with nearly identical global reionization histories. The data favor an escape fraction that decreases with increasing redshift, from $\approx 0.8$ at $z = 5$ to $\approx 0.35$ at $z = 15$. The halo-mass-only model prefers $f_{\rm esc}$ increasing with halo mass, but this trend acts as a proxy for redshift evolution. When we vary both dependencies jointly, the data prefer a mass-independent $f_{\rm esc}$. At matched global neutral fraction, the ionization morphology is closely similar for all four prescriptions, and the 21 cm power spectra agree to within $\approx 10\%$. These results suggest that, once calibrated against the same observations, the details of the $f_{\rm esc}$ prescription, which are set by the physics of the interstellar medium, largely average out in both the global observables and the 21 cm power spectrum. Distinguishing them may require statistics beyond the power spectrum, such as sightline statistics of the Ly$\alpha$ and 21 cm forests, or forecasts that exploit their small differences in reionization timing.

The authors parameterize $f_{\rm esc}$ as power-law functions of redshift $z$, halo mass $M_{\rm h}$, and both jointly, and constrain them against JWST UV luminosity functions and EoR data (ionizing emissivity, neutral hydrogen fraction, and CMB Thomson optical depth) using MCMC. They then propagate the calibrated models into the semi-numerical simulation SimFast21 to assess the spatial ionization bubble morphology and 21 cm power spectra compared to a constant-$f_{\rm esc}$ baseline. They find that global observables and 21 cm power spectra are remarkably degenerate across different escape fraction prescriptions once calibrated to the same data.
conclusions: Observational data strongly favor an escape fraction that declines with increasing redshift, dropping from $f_{\rm esc} \approx 0.8$ at $z = 5$ to $\approx 0.35$ at $z = 15$, effectively resolving the JWST photon budget crisis.

At matched global neutral fractions, the 3D ionization morphologies are visually very similar across all prescriptions, and the 21 cm power spectra agree to within $\approx 10\%$ (with deviations $<2\%$ for the mass-only model relative to constant $f_{\rm esc}$).

Because large-scale 21 cm power spectrum measurements average out the small-scale interstellar medium physics of $f_{\rm esc}$, distinguishing physical escape fraction models will require higher-order statistics (such as the bispectrum), sightline statistics (Ly$\alpha$ and 21 cm forest), or precise timing measurements from SKA-Low.

papers.title: ECH0EZ: Estimating the Hubble constant with ZTF SN Ia DR2
papers.authors: Konstantin Karchev, Marco Giunta, Raul Jimenez, Roberto Trotta, Licia Verde
papers.abstract: Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are instrumental for a precise measurement of the Hubble constant ($H_0$) from the local distance ladder, yet the data used hitherto for this purpose are inhomogeneous and subject to severe selection effects. We present the first, preliminary, cosmological analysis of 772 SNe Ia from the Zwicky Transient Facility's second data release: an untargeted single-telescope sample whose volume-limited subset (z<0.06) is largely free of Malmquist bias. We correct the public data for known instrumental and calibration biases and the redshifts for peculiar motions. Using the 42 SH0ES calibrators (their host distances computed from Cepheids and geometric anchors) and a Bayesian hierarchical model of SN Ia standardisation, dust extinction, redshift and calibration uncertainties, we infer $H_0 = (71.6 \pm 1.5)$ km/s/Mpc after marginalising over deceleration with a flat prior (or $(72.3 \pm 1.1)$ km/s/Mpc if a prior on matter density from Pantheon+ is imposed), with the uncertainty dominated by the number of calibrators. We demonstrate robustness to the choice of light-curve and Milky Way dust models and to extensions of the model to include peculiar-velocity correlations, a host-mass step, and two stretch populations. These results are in agreement with previous distance-ladder measurements and $2.7\sigma$ ($4.1\sigma$) away from the value obtained from Planck data, suggesting that the resolution of the Hubble tension lies outside of SNe Ia---or the distance ladder entirely.

Their findings yield local $H_0$ measurements consistent with previous distance-ladder studies, indicating that selection effects in SN Ia samples are unlikely to be the primary cause of the Hubble tension.

papers.title: All Dark Matter as Primordial Black Holes: a Gravitational-Wave Test
papers.authors: A. Ianniccari, A. J. Iovino, G. Perna, D. Perrone, A. Riotto
papers.abstract: We propose a novel test for the hypothesis that the dark matter of the Universe is composed entirely by asteroidal-mass primordial black holes. It relies on detecting the stochastic gravitational-wave background generated by the coalescence onto rapidly spinning supermassive astrophysical black holes of the light primordial black holes accumulated in spherically symmetric spikes. We discuss the scenarios in which the signal can be observed by the future space-based gravitational-wave observatories LISA and DECIGO.

To model this, they evaluate the inclination-averaged GW energy flux using the Teukolsky perturbation framework for spherical Kerr geodesics, alongside a simplified analytical model for equatorial prograde orbits. The results show that while individual inspirals are unresolvable, their cosmic superposition could be detectable by DECIGO across standard parameters, and by LISA if the central dark matter spike is sufficiently steep ($\,\gamma \gtrsim 2.5$).

papers.title: Non-minimal $α$-attractor magnetogenesis with potential dependent couplings
papers.authors: Antonino G. Marino, Tommaso Mengoni
papers.abstract: We investigate inflationary magnetogenesis driven by a non conformal coupling in the case of large-field $\alpha$-attractor inspired models. We introduce potential-dependent electromagnetic coupling functions $f(\phi)$ that reproduce the scaling $f\propto a^p$ during slow roll. Starting from Starobinsky inflation, we analytically derive explicit couplings for $(E)$-model and $(T)$-model potentials. We then study how these functions affect electromagnetic amplification in the regime of non-minimal coupling between the inflaton field and the Ricci scalar $\phi^2 R$. In particular, we compare different values for the coupling strength $\xi$, accounting for electromagnetic backreaction and Schwinger pair production through the gradient expansion formalism. Our numerical results show that the non-minimal coupling affects the evolution of the electromagnetic sector and the resulting magnetic-field amplitude. We find that, within the analyzed configurations, minimally coupled and $\xi>0$ scenarios are compatible with the adopted CMB constraints, yielding conditional present-day magnetic-field estimates of order $10^{-23}$ G.

They evaluate the impact of the non-minimal coupling strength $\xi$ on electromagnetic amplification and constrain parameter space using CMB observables ($n_s$, $r$). They find that minimally coupled ($\xi=0$) and positive non-minimal coupling ($\xi>0$) models satisfy CMB constraints and produce seed magnetic fields of order $10^{-23}\text{ G}$ at the present day, whereas negative coupling ($\xi<0$) yields red-tilted spectra inconsistent with CMB bounds.

papers.title: Towards Reliably Measuring the Mass-Size Relation of Dark Matter Halos: Impact of projection, miscentering and Eddington bias
papers.authors: Charlie T. Mpetha, Benedikt Diemer
papers.abstract: In the conventional spherical overdensity definition of a dark matter halo, masses and radii, e.g. $M_{200{\rm m}}$ and $r_{200{\rm m}}$, are equivalent. However, halos do exhibit a physical boundary at the splashback radius $r_{\rm sp}$, which manifests as a sharp drop in density. Splashback radii are now routinely measured in stacked weak lensing profiles, but the expected trend of decreasing $r_{\rm sp}/r_{200{\rm m}}$ with mass has not been verified in observed galaxy groups or clusters. In this work, we show that several observational effects conceal the predicted mass-size relation. In particular, we quantify the impact of systematics on the mean density and lensing profiles of mock-observed halo samples, which are created by applying a realistic cluster-finding procedure to dark matter-only simulations. We reproduce the known impact of projection: preferentially observing systems in overdense regions. But, differing from previous works, we show that the same projection effect, combined with scatter in observed luminosities, causes a significant Eddington bias in the derived mass-observable relation and a complex suppression in mean density profiles over all radial scales. The magnitude of this effect is mass-dependent and coupled to the cluster-finding procedure and survey properties, making it challenging to model simply and motivating full forward-modeling of observed group and cluster samples. However, we demonstrate that a simple mitigation approach, effectively a weak lensing mass calibration, does well in approximately recovering the true mass-size relation. Finally, we show that only severe miscentering can bias the measurement of the halo size, but any miscentering can increase the measurement uncertainty.

To explain this discrepancy, the authors constructed mock-observed cluster catalogs from the Erebos dark-matter simulation suite by applying realistic cluster-finding algorithms, subhalo abundance matching, luminosity scatter, projection, and miscentering. They found that Eddington bias from scatter in mass proxies, combined with projection effects, suppresses the stacked density and weak lensing profiles by up to $\sim 40\%$, thereby obscuring the true physical halo mass-size relation.

The combined impact of projection and selection systematics depresses stacked lensing profiles by up to $\sim 40\%$ across all radial scales, severely biasing inferred halo radii and concealing the theoretical $r_{\rm t}/r_{200\rm m}$ mass trend.

papers.title: Warm inflation beyond the Gaussian limit: primordial black holes and induced gravitational waves
papers.authors: Mayukh R. Gangopadhyay, Nilanjana Kumar
papers.abstract: In warm inflation, the primordial fluctuations are driven by random kicks from a hot radiation bath. Two features of these kicks matter: how long the bath remembers them, which shapes the power spectrum, and how their strengths are spread, which controls the rare, extreme fluctuations. In this paper, we investigate how primordial black holes and the accompanying induced gravitational waves can be used to discriminate between these two features. We use a simple model inspired by warm inflation, in which independent kicks of random strength add up to a narrow peak in the power spectrum. At leading order, the induced gravitational wave depends only on the power spectrum and is therefore insensitive to how the kicks are distributed. However, the black holes are very sensitive to these rare large fluctuations. Hence, two baths can yield the same gravitational wave signal while forming black holes at very different rates. A modest kurtosis range of 0.1 to 0.3 enhances black-hole formation by factors of ten to a million at fixed gravitational-wave amplitude, the larger factors for the rarer black holes. Counting peaks rather than all points, or widening the spectrum, lowers the enhancement by at most a factor of about four. In general a change in the power affects both phenomena, while the kurtosis affects only the black hole production.

A modest primordial excess kurtosis of $K = 0.1$ to $0.3$ increases the PBH collapse probability by factors of $10^{0.9}$ to $10^{6.2}$ at fixed SIGW signal amplitude, with the strongest enhancement occurring for the rarest peaks.

papers.title: Relativistic N-body simulations with mass-varying neutrinos
papers.authors: Øyvind Christiansen, Julian Adamek, Mainak Baidya, Vitor da Fonseca, Eric V. Linder, David F. Mota
papers.abstract: Recent cosmological data provide weak hints for smaller masses than what is required by neutrino-oscillation experiments, motivating investigations into variation of the neutrino masses with cosmic time. Here we study a model where the neutrinos couple to a quintessence field that acts as dark energy. We compute structure formation using fully dynamical and relativistic N-body and lattice simulations, with nonlinear field evolution and a weak-field metric expansion. Similar to previous studies, we find the generic appearance of neutrino lumps, but observe them to be highly dynamical and spinning. We study several models where the effective dark energy, including nonlinear effects of the scalar field on the cosmic expansion, can show phantom crossing. The relativistic physics available in our simulation framework can help distinguish such models from LCDM, through observations of neutrino and dark energy properties, and slip between the gravitational potentials due to anisotropic stress. The rich phenomenology offered by mass-varying neutrinos motivates further exploration and development of the simulation techniques.

papers.title: Cosmological constraints on single-field inflation models from ACT/SPT data and observations at sub-Mpc scales
papers.authors: Qing-Yang Wang, Jing-Zhi Zhou, Fei-Yu Chen, Zhi-Chao Li
papers.abstract: We investigate single-field inflation models that can produce large curvature perturbations at sub-Mpc scales while remaining consistent with cosmological observations across multiple regimes. We highlight the tension between generating enhanced small-scale perturbations and maintaining agreement with the scalar spectral index $n_s$ measured by ACT and SPT, which disfavors several conventional single-field inflation models. To address this issue, we propose three viable classes of inflationary potentials: bump/dip-modified, step-like, and double-inflection-point. Each can sufficiently amplify primordial perturbations while predicting $n_s$ that lie within the $2\sigma$ range of current observational bounds. In addition, we examine the primordial power spectra predicted by these models and constrain their parameter spaces using cosmological observations at different scales, including CMB, BAO, PBH, PTA, and CMB-distortion. Our results show that some of the models considered can simultaneously satisfy the ACT/SPT constraints and account for the current PTA observations, although doing so while respecting the constraints on the PBH abundance remains challenging.

papers.title: Getting Ready For Analysing Rubin Data : CLMM v2, The Updated LSST-DESC Cluster Weak Lensing Mass Modeling Library For Cosmology
papers.authors: Michel Aguena, Céline Combet, Shenming Fu, Constantin Payerne, Marina Ricci, Camille Avestruz, Eduardo Barroso, de Oliveira Caio, Zhou Conghao, Hsin Fan, Calum Murray, Anna Niemiec, Nikolina Sarcevic, Tae-hyeon Shin, Rance Solomon, Radhakrishnan Srinivasan, Sunayama Tomomi, Yuanyuan Zhang, Joe Zuntz

Here, we present the methodology to constrain the mass information of galaxy clusters from weak lensing, which is encompassed by the v2.0 release of the Cluster Lensing Mass Modeling (CLMM) code. papers.title: A self-supervised machine learning approach to identify instrumental systematics in 21cm Cosmology
papers.authors: Ajith Sampath
papers.abstract: The primordial sound waves in the baryon-photon plasma are imprinted on the large-scale galaxy distribution as Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO), serving as a cosmological standard ruler to constrain dark energy and the Hubble parameter. The upcoming 21cm intensity-mapping arrays are designed to map the 21cm emission across large volumes and measure the BAO scale. However, radio interferometers suffer from instrumental systematics that can hinder detection of the cosmological 21cm signal by leaking bright foregrounds into the signal-dominated modes. This work aims to demonstrate that a self-supervised model can predict the instrument systematic state (here, the amplitude of a spectral ripple in the beam width) in interferometric visibilities and potentially disentangle the instrument from the sky without a forward model. Based on the fact that an instrument stays the same as the sky rotates in a drift-scan observation, and that the same sky is observed under different instrument states, we train a convolutional autoencoder to compress the information in the simulated visibilities and separate this information into instrument-only and sky-only latent vectors. The result shows excellent prediction of the unknown instrument systematic for 15 held-out instrument states with $R^2 = 0.9975$ with a linear probe, against $R^2 = -3.55$ for a random-encoder baseline. The instrument-latent carries no detectable sky signal, as measured with a total-power sky proxy, for any held-out test data. The sky-latent vector and instrument-latent vector show partial separation but not complete disentanglement, identifying sky-latent purity as the primary open problem. The results show the ability of the model to recognize the systematic and show a promising path towards an ML-based foreground cleaning pipeline. Full instrument-sky disentanglement constitutes the natural next step.

papers.title: Cosmological Constraints on Interacting Dark Matter with SPT-3G D1
papers.authors: Cynthia Trendafilova, Fei Ge, Ali Rida Khalife, Christian L. Reichardt
papers.abstract: Models of the dark sector in which the dark matter participates in nontrivial interactions can create detectable signatures in cosmological observables, providing non-terrestrial means of probing the nature of dark matter. In this work, we test dark matter-baryon scattering, dark matter-dark radiation interactions, and dark matter annihilation using measurements of the CMB and BAO. We leverage the latest SPT-3G D1 CMB measurements of the primary anisotropies, alongside the D1 MUSE lensing data, to set up-to-date bounds on these models. From the combination of Planck, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 data, we constrain the velocity-independent dark matter-baryon scattering cross-section to $\sigma_\mathrm{DM-b} < 4.6\times10^{-26}~\mathrm{cm^2}$, the dark matter-dark radiation momentum transfer rate to $\Gamma_\mathrm{0,nadm}<5.2\times10^{-8}\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$, and the effective dark matter annihilation parameter, quantifying the fractional thermally averaged cross-section, to $p_\mathrm{ann}<3.7\times10^{-28}~\mathrm{cm^3/s/GeV}$, all at the 95% confidence level. The improved sensitivity to the first two models is in particular driven by the precision measurements of CMB lensing at small scales provided by SPT-3G D1 MUSE lensing data. For annihilating dark matter, due to the degeneracy of the effect with the optical depth to reionization, we observe a non-trivial relationship between the upper bound on $p_\mathrm{ann}$ and the large-scale polarization information. When combining CMB data with the latest measurements from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), upper bounds on extended model parameters can appear to tighten as the model space attempts to accommodate the known discrepancy between these data. Future CMB and BAO measurements will provide better clarity on reconciling this discrepancy and enhance our ability to test dark matter interactions.

papers.title: Improving cosmological distance measurements at high redshift using Lyman-Alpha forest BAO reconstruction
papers.authors: Boryana Hadzhiyska, Roger de Belsunce
papers.abstract: The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) measures baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) in the Lyman-$\alpha$ (Lyman-alpha) forest and provides a robust probe of the expansion history in the matter-dominated era. Yet, non-linear structure formation broadens and shifts the BAO peak. To undo these effects, we extend standard Zel'dovich reconstruction, routinely applied to galaxy surveys, to the Lyman-alpha forest. We validate our methodology on large-volume idealized Lyman-alpha forest mocks painted on top of the \textsc{AbacusSummit} $N$-body simulations, using linear control variates to suppress sample variance and thereby reduce the error bars by a factor of up to $\approx \sqrt{50}$. In fully sampled periodic boxes, reconstruction halves the radial BAO damping scale and reduces the uncertainties on the radial ($\apar$) and transverse ($\aperp$) scaling parameters by $\approx25\%$ and $\approx15\%$, respectively. It also reduces the non-linear shift from $\Delta\apar=+0.3\%$ to $+0.10\pm0.07\%$, while $\aperp$ remains unbiased. To make this approach readily applicable to observational data, we demonstrate the impact of a survey mask with a DESI-like density of $50\,\mathrm{deg}^{-2}$. For this mask, we compare two approaches to estimate the displacement field: either directly from the Lyman-alpha forest or using an external tracer with a number density of $\bar n \simeq 10^{-3}\,h^3\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$, such as Lyman-break galaxies and Lyman-$\alpha$ emitters---both key targets for DESI-II. Both approaches give comparable gains and reduce the uncertainties on $\apar$ and $\aperp$ by $\approx 27\%$ and $\approx 10\%$, respectively, with mild improvements for futuristic high-density surveys with $160\,\mathrm{deg}^{-2}$. Correspondingly, the figure of merit improves by factors of $1.66$ for fully sampled boxes, $1.65$ for a DESI-like, and $1.76$ for a high-density survey.

papers.title: Axions from Betelgeuse: Probing Axion Couplings with $^{23}\rm{Na}$ and $^{55}\rm{Mn}$
papers.authors: Nicholas A. M. Revel, Baldeep Grewal, Anupam Ray, Aaron C. Vincent
papers.abstract: We investigate axion-like particle (ALP) production in the interior of Betelgeuse via nuclear de-excitation of thermally populated excited states of $^{23}$Na and $^{55}$Mn. As these ALPs propagate to Earth, they can produce photons either through their conversion in the Galactic magnetic field or through their decay. Using INTEGRAL-ISGRI and NuSTAR observations, we search for these photon signals, find no significant excess, and derive 95% CL exclusion limits on the ALP couplings. For magnetic-field conversion of ALPs, the $^{23}\mathrm{Na}$ ($^{55}\mathrm{Mn}$) line observed with INTEGRAL-ISGRI constrains $|g_{a\gamma}g_{ap}| < 4.1\times10^{-21}$ ($6.9\times10^{-19}$) $\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$ for $m_a < 10^{-10} \mathrm{eV}$. For ALP decays, the $^{23}\mathrm{Na}$ ($^{55}\mathrm{Mn}$) line observed with INTEGRAL-ISGRI (NuSTAR) constrains $|g_{a\gamma}g_{ap}|$ down to $3.0\times10^{-22}$ ($2.9\times10^{-19}$) $\mathrm{GeV}^{-1}$ at $m_a \simeq 400$ ($83$) keV, weakening in both cases as $m_a^{-3/2}$ for lower ALP masses, and as $m_a^{-2}$ for $^{23}$Na below $m_a \sim 1$ keV, with sensitivity extending to $m_a \simeq 440.2$ ($124$) keV. Although our $^{23}\mathrm{Na}$-based limits are the strongest for both channels, their larger transition energy makes them more sensitive to the precise evolutionary stage of Betelgeuse, whereas the $^{55}\mathrm{Mn}$-based limits are considerably more robust against such uncertainties.

papers.abstract: SIRMOS is a mission concept for a future NASA Astrophysics Explorer opportunity that aims to revolutionize our understanding of the universe by mapping the large-scale structure of galaxies in unprecedented breadth and detail to explore cosmic origins and evolution. Specifically, the primary science goals of SIRMOS are to discover how cosmic inflation seeded large-scale structure, reveal the nature of the accelerating expansion of the universe, and measure the sum of neutrino masses to exceptionally high precision. Its secondary science goals include determining how environment shapes galaxy evolution at cosmic noon and beyond, and probing the Milky Way's dust-enshrouded regions, reaching the far side of our Galaxy. To accomplish its transformative science goals, SIRMOS executes a 3-year cosmology survey over the Euclid footprint of ~14,000 deg$^2$, obtaining slit spectra for ~100 million galaxies at 1<z<4. SIRMOS is the first space mission designed specifically to leverage Euclid's wide near-infrared (IR) imaging survey for target selection and employs a digital micro-mirror device (DMD) to acquire up to 4,000 simultaneous spectra over a wide 0.9 deg$^2$ field of view. The instrument's excellent spectral resolution of $R=1300$ and continuous wavelength coverage from 1.25--2.5 $\mu$m capture the redshifts of distant galaxies with no gaps, reducing systematic biases to achieve ground-breaking science.

papers.title: Derivation of OH sum rules without Rayleigh--Jeans approximation: a powerful tool for measuring the variation of fundamental physical constants
papers.authors: Renzhi Su, Minfeng Gu
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that the optical depths of any OH $\Lambda$-doublet quartet obey one exact linear relation in every velocity channel. No approximation is needed. The only exception is the $^{2}\Pi_{1/2}$ $J{=}1/2$ level, which has three transitions only, because its $F{=}0{\leftrightarrow}0$ line is strictly forbidden. The relation is $\tau_{S_1}(v)/\mu_{S_1}^{2}+\tau_{S_2}(v)/\mu_{S_2}^{2}=\tau_{M_1}(v)/(a\mu_{M_1}^{2})+\tau_{M_2}(v)/(b\mu_{M_2}^{2})$, where $a=2J^{2}+J-1$, $b=2J^{2}+3J$, and the $\mu_i^{2}$ are reduced transition dipole moments derived from the catalogued Einstein $A$ coefficients. It holds equally for gas in local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE), for non-LTE gas, for masers and for conjugate gas. We suggest that it is a powerful tool for measuring the variation of fundamental physical constants.

papers.title: Can inflationary axion fluctuations dominate over misalignment?
papers.authors: Seung J. Lee, Sarunas Verner, Bingrong Yu
papers.abstract: The relic abundance of light stable axion dark matter is usually set by misalignment. We study whether the inflationary fluctuations of the axion can dominate instead, and we follow the modes analytically through an instantaneous transition from de Sitter expansion to radiation domination, neglecting the axion mass during inflation and keeping it afterward. Since the energy density is quadratic in the field, a fluctuation-dominated abundance carries an isocurvature perturbation even when the mean displacement vanishes. For a canonical minimally coupled axion the spectrum is scale invariant, and fluctuation-dominated dark matter exceeds the Planck isocurvature limit by about eight orders of magnitude. An inflaton-dependent kinetic function or a nonminimal coupling to the Ricci scalar tilts the spectrum blue, moving the fluctuation power from CMB scales to small scales. Imposing the Planck limit at the pivot scale, we find that fluctuation-dominated dark matter with a constant kinetic slope requires the spectral tilt $n_\eta-1\gtrsim0.27$ and the axion mass $m_{\eta} \gtrsim200 \rm{GeV}$ at $H_I=10^{10}\rm{GeV}$, and $n_\eta-1\gtrsim0.34$ and $m_\eta\gtrsim4.5\,$keV at $H_I=10^{13}\rm{GeV}$. A kinetic function with a running slope lowers these masses to $1.4~\rm{GeV}$ and $0.7\,$eV, respectively. For the QCD axion, whose oscillations start late, we estimate that any single power-law spectrum blue enough to satisfy the pivot limit gives too little fluctuation abundance, and misalignment dominates.

papers.title: Dark Matter Coherent Freeze-Out Mechanism: A Comprehensive Analysis
papers.authors: Steven Ferrante, Lillian Luo, Maxim Perelstein, Bingrong Yu
papers.abstract: Both Weakly-Interacting Massive Particle (WIMP) and Axion-Like Particle (ALP) are attractive particle dark matter candidates. In this paper we consider a scenario in which both WIMP and ALP are present. The two species interact via a non-derivative quadratic coupling modeled on the axion-nucleon interaction in QCD. We show that even a small (Planck-suppressed) coupling can drastically modify the cosmological history of both species. In the very early Universe, the ALP field acquires a vacuum expectation value, and the system undergoes an inverse phase transition at a temperature around or below the weak scale. WIMPs may remain in equilibrium far beyond the usual freeze-out time, eventually decoupling via a novel "coherent freeze-out" mechanism. WIMP annihilation cross sections several orders of magnitude above the canonical thermal target value can be consistent with the observed relic density in the coherent freeze-out scenario. At the same time, coherent oscillations of the ALP field do not begin until after the phase transition, and the initial conditions for these oscillations are set by the thermal physics of the phase transition. The ALP relic density is then predicted unambiguously in terms of the WIMP mass and coupling. We term this scenario "ALP miracle", since the observed relic density is obtained when these parameters are around their natural values, the weak and the Planck scale. The ALP miracle scenario prefers the ALP mass above about $10^{-3}\,\mathrm{eV}$, far larger than other popular ALP dark matter models. The ALP miracle parameter space overlaps with a currently allowed region of the QCD axion band, a large fraction of which is expected to be probed by the proposed IAXO experiment.

Their defining signature is a central $g-r$ color at least 0.2 mag bluer than the reference population within $a=20$ kpc before returning to the normal BCG envelope. Ha emission equivalent width correlates strongly with the blue continuum excess, consistent with young stellar components comprising ~0.1-1% of pre-existing stellar mass. Line ratios indicate widespread LINER-like excitation, with a larger star-forming contribution in blue Ha emitters but substantial non-stellar excitation. This activity is closely linked to the thermodynamics of the host-cluster gas. At $0.1R_{500}$, cooling times decrease from BCGs without significant Ha emission to red and then blue Ha emitters. Blue BCGs preferentially occur in clusters with $L_{\rm X,300}>10^{44}$ erg s$^{-1}$; red Ha emitters also favor higher X-ray luminosities. The blue-core fraction rises with optical richness. For systems with $t_{\rm cool}(0.1R_{500})<20$ Gyr, doubling richness increases the odds of hosting a blue-core BCG by $2.45\pm0.39$. This indicates that cluster scale carries information beyond cooling time, plausibly through the amount of gas available for cooling and condensation. The scarcity of blue BCGs without significant Ha emission disfavors isolated short bursts followed by long Ha-quiet fading phases. It can instead be explained by sustained or closely recurrent star formation over timescales much longer than 100 Myr, or by Ha persisting through additional excitation mechanisms as the young stellar component fades.

Using X-ray data from the eROSITA All-Sky Survey (eRASS:5) combined with optical imaging from the Legacy Surveys, the authors identified 379 blue-core BCGs out of a sample of over 11,000 clusters at $z < 0.6$. They analyzed the relationship between these blue cores, optical emission lines (like H$\alpha$), and the thermodynamic state of the surrounding ICM to understand how gas cooling and AGN feedback regulate galaxy growth. The study reveals that while short cooling times are necessary, the overall scale of the cluster (richness) also plays a significant role in determining the presence of a blue-core BCG.

papers.title: A Point-source Catalogue from Direction-dependent Calibrated 21CMA Images
papers.authors: Qizhe Tang, Jingying Wang, Junhua Gu, Qian Zheng, Quan Guo, Tingyan Shen, Bixuan Zhao, Qiuyi Lai, Yan Huang, Kuanjun Li, Yang Feng
papers.abstract: We present a deep low-frequency radio point-source catalogue centred on the North Celestial Pole (NCP) and extending $5^\circ$ in radius, derived from a single 24-h observation with the 21 CentiMeter Array (21CMA). Covering 75-175 MHz, the catalogue characterises extragalactic foreground point sources for Epoch of Reionization (EoR) studies. Previous 21CMA imaging has been limited by reduced dynamic range caused by direction-dependent effects, particularly the severe grating lobes of ultra-bright sources such as 3C 61.1 and ionospheric phase distortions. Here we apply 21CMAcali, a direction-dependent calibration and imaging pipeline, to mitigate these effects. The angular resolution ranges from 2.3 arcmin at 100 MHz to 1.4 arcmin at 168.75 MHz. The resulting maps show reduced artefacts and background noise, enabling more reliable recovery of faint sources. We construct a catalogue of 1246 radio point sources. Cross-matching with LoTSS-DR3, WENSS, and NVSS enables broad-band spectral fitting, while an independent in-band analysis yields a median spectral index of $\alpha=-0.825$ (where $S \propto \nu^{\alpha}$). The Euclidean-normalised differential source counts at 150 MHz, derived from a dedicated 50-MHz-wide multi-frequency synthesis (MFS) image, are broadly consistent with existing measurements and semi-empirical models at the bright end, whereas the deficit at lower flux densities ($S \lesssim 0.04$ Jy) mainly reflects limited sensitivity and incompleteness. This catalogue improves foreground point-source characterisation in the 21CMA NCP field, demonstrates the value of direction-dependent calibration, and provides a reference for deeper catalogues based on multi-day observations.

ai.summary: This paper presents a new radio point-source catalogue from the 21 CentiMeter Array (21CMA), focusing on the North Celestial Pole (NCP) region at 75–175 MHz. The authors address a common challenge in low-frequency radio astronomy: direction-dependent effects (DDEs) caused by ionospheric distortions and the 'grating lobes' (interference patterns) of extremely bright sources like 3C 61.1, which typically limit the dynamic range of images. By applying a direction-dependent calibration pipeline (21CMAcali), they successfully mitigated these artefacts, allowing for the detection of 1246 sources. This work is primarily a technical and observational effort to characterize foregrounds that must be removed to eventually detect the much fainter 21-cm signal from the Epoch of Reionization (EoR).

Achieved a median spectral index of $\alpha = -0.825$, consistent with standard extragalactic synchrotron emission.
Demonstrated that direction-dependent calibration (DDC) improves the image dynamic range by factors of 1.2 to 2.0 compared to standard calibration.
Improved astrometric accuracy by more than an order of magnitude relative to previous 21CMA catalogues.
Found that Euclidean-normalised source counts at 150 MHz are consistent with semi-empirical models at the bright end ($S > 0.04$ Jy).

papers.title: Weighing dark matter particles with gravitational waves
papers.authors: Rodrigo Vicente, Francisco Duque, Theophanes K. Karydas, Gianfranco Bertone
papers.abstract: It is commonly assumed that the mass of dark matter particles cannot be determined from their gravitational effects when dark matter behaves as collisionless matter. Here we show that extreme-mass-ratio inspirals observable by millihertz gravitational-wave observatories such as the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) could measure the mass of ultralight dark matter particles in sufficiently dense dark matter spikes. The separation of scales between the two black holes allows ultralight dark matter to form a collisionless density spike around the massive primary while retaining wave effects in its interaction with the stellar-mass companion. We incorporate wave-dependent accretion and dynamical friction into relativistic inspiral waveforms and jointly infer the dark matter particle mass, spike normalisation and binary parameters from simulated LISA signals. For massive black holes at the low-mass end of the LISA population ($M\sim 10^5 M_\odot$), our forecasts show that particle masses spanning $10^{-14}-10^{-11}\,\mathrm{eV}$ could be measured to within an order of magnitude.

ai.summary: This paper investigates the potential for the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) to measure the mass of ultralight dark matter (ULDM) particles by observing Extreme-Mass-Ratio Inspirals (EMRIs)—systems where a stellar-mass compact object orbits a massive black hole. In these systems, ULDM can form a dense 'spike' that behaves as a collisionless fluid on the scale of the primary black hole but exhibits wave-like effects (such as modified dynamical friction and accretion) on the scale of the smaller companion. By incorporating these wave-dependent effects into relativistic waveforms, the authors demonstrate that the resulting phase shifts in the gravitational wave signal can be used to break the degeneracy between the dark matter distribution and the particle's microscopic mass.
conclusions: LISA could measure ULDM particle masses in the range $10^{-14}$ to $10^{-11}$ eV to within an order of magnitude for systems with $M \sim 10^5 M_\odot$.
The dark matter particle mass $m_\phi$ and the spike normalization $\bar{\rho}$ are correlated, but the unique radial dependence of wave-driven torques allows for their joint inference.
Sensitivity is highest for low-mass primaries ($M \lesssim 2 \times 10^5 M_\odot$) where environmental effects are stronger relative to gravitational radiation reaction at larger radii.
Extending LISA's observation time from 4 to 8 years significantly lowers the host halo density required to make a definitive mass measurement.
For masses above $10^{-11}$ eV, the interaction approaches the collisionless limit, allowing for precise density constraints but only lower bounds on the particle mass.

papers.title: Measuring the magnetization profiles of galaxy groups and clusters
papers.authors: Kritti Sharma, Vikram Ravi, Elisabeth Krause
papers.abstract: Magnetic fields are vital in determining the physical conditions of baryons in massive halos. They are, however, notoriously difficult to observe. This impacts problems from our understanding of galaxy formation, to the observed deficit in the amplitude of thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) power spectrum that affects cosmological inferences. Although Faraday rotation measures (RMs) offer a direct probe of magnetic fields, it weights magnetic fields by the free-electron density. Several probes of free electrons, including fast radio burst (FRB) dispersion measures (DMs) and kinematic SZ (kSZ) effect, are now maturing into precision tools. We combine RM$^2$ stacks from SPICE-RACS around DESI galaxy groups and ROSAT clusters with optical depth profiles constrained jointly by the FRB DM-redshift relation and the kSZ effect, and obtain 95% upper limits on the rms line-of-sight magnetic field of $<3.9$-$11.6~\mu$G ($<2.3$-$6.4~\mu$G) in groups (clusters) for a 10~kpc coherence length. Combining these with thermal pressure profiles inferred from tSZ-shear cross-correlations, we obtain 95% lower limits on the plasma $\beta$ of $>0.31$ ($>11$) in groups (clusters). Although current constraints are only limits, we forecast a first detection with larger datasets from the Deep Synoptic Array (DSA). We present the first forecast of the DSA RM grid density ($\sim365$ RMs deg$^{-2}$), which when combined with 10$^4$ FRBs would measure the field in groups to $3$-$13\%$ precision, compared to current constraints of $38$-$75\%$. Although the interpretation of current measurements remains challenging owing to depolarization along turbulent halo sightlines and the unknown coherence length, larger samples and DSA/Square Kilometer Array observations may resolve these uncertainties by measuring polarization-fraction profiles and the RM structure function using extended radio sources, respectively.

The authors break this degeneracy by combining $RM^2$ stacks from the SPICE-RACS survey with independent electron density profiles derived from Fast Radio Burst (FRB) dispersion measures and the kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) effect. By further incorporating thermal pressure profiles from tSZ-shear cross-correlations, they provide new constraints on the magnetic field strength and the plasma $\beta$ (the ratio of thermal to magnetic pressure) in massive halos. This is particularly relevant for understanding the 'tSZ deficit'—a discrepancy where observed tSZ signals are lower than predicted—which may be partially explained by non-thermal pressure support from magnetic fields.
conclusions: Obtained 95% upper limits on the rms line-of-sight magnetic field of $<3.9$-$11.6\,\mu$G for galaxy groups and $<2.3$-$6.4\,\mu$G for clusters (assuming a 10 kpc coherence length).
Derived 95% lower limits on the plasma $\beta$ of $>0.31$ for groups and $>11$ for clusters, suggesting magnetic pressure in clusters is at most $\approx 10\%$ of thermal pressure.
Found that current cluster RM profiles from SPICE-RACS are significantly lower than IllustrisTNG predictions, likely due to Faraday depolarization and selection effects in polarized source catalogs.
Forecasts for the Deep Synoptic Array (DSA) suggest that $10^4$ localized FRBs and a dense RM grid will improve magnetic field precision in groups to $3$-$13\%$, enabling a first detection.

papers.title: Sym-EFT: Accelerating Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure with Symbolic Regression
papers.authors: Despoina Farakou, Constantinos Skordis
papers.abstract: We present an emulator suite for the one- and two-loop cold dark matter power spectrum from the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structures (EFTofLSS). Specifically, we emulate separately the various contributions to the one- and two-loop parts of the power spectrum, leaving out the possible counterterms which can be added as multiplicative prefactors. By leaving the time-dependence of the counterterms unspecified at the emulation stage, our technique has the advantage of being extremely versatile in fitting any type of counterterm parametrisation to data, or to simulations, without having to change the emulator. We construct our emulators using the method of symbolic regression which results in functions that can be used directly in computer code, while achieving errors of better than $0.5\%$ within the $k$-range of validity of EFT and maintaining ultra-fast computational evaluation of less than $\sim5\times10^{-4}s$ on a single core.

papers.title: Heavy Black-Holes Also Matter in Standard Siren Cosmology
papers.authors: Grégoire Pierra, Alexander Papadopoulos
papers.abstract: With the release of the Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog GWTC-4.0 by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) collaboration, 218 candidate detections of gravitational waves (GWs) from compact binary coalescences (CBCs) have been reported. This milestone represents a major advancement for GW cosmology, as many methods, particularly those employing the spectral siren approach, critically depend on the number of available sources. We investigate the impact of a novel parametric model describing the full population mass spectrum of CBCs on the estimation of the Hubble constant. This model is designed to test the impact of heavy black holes in GW cosmology. We perform a joint inference of cosmological and population parameters using 142 CBCs from GWTC-4.0 with a false alarm rate smaller than 0.25 per year, using both spectral and dark siren approaches. With spectral sirens, we estimate the Hubble constant to be $H_0 = 78.8^{+19.0}_{-15.3}\,{\rm km s^{-1} Mpc^{-1}}$ (68% CL), while the dark siren method yields $H_0 = 82.5^{+16.8}_{-14.3}\,{\rm km s^{-1} Mpc^{-1}}$ (68% CL). These results improve the uncertainty by approximately 30.4% and 36.2%, respectively. We show that this improvement is linked to the presence of a new mass scale in the binary black hole mass spectrum at $63.3^{+4.8}_{-4.8}\,M_{\odot}$, which provides additional constraints on the Hubble constant. Besides providing the tightest standard-siren constraints on $H_0$, this highlights the importance of a heavy-mass feature in the black hole spectrum.

papers.title: Extracting intrinsic alignments in the Dark Energy Survey's year 1 data, using the self-calibration method and LSST-DESC tools
papers.authors: Eske M. Pedersen, Leonel Medina-Varela, Emily Phillips Longley, Mustapha Ishak, Joe Zuntz, Chihway Chang, C. Danielle Leonard (for the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration (LSST DESC))
papers.abstract: We present the implementation of a Self-Calibration of Intrinsic Alignments of galaxies as an extension to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) Dark Energy Science Collaboration (DESC)'s weak lensing 3x2pt pipeline (TXPipe). As a demonstration, we have run this pipeline on the Dark Energy Survey (DES) year one data set. We find indications of a non-zero intrinsic alignment signal in the higher redshift bins, while in the lower bins our results look more uncertain. We believe this is caused by known issues with the individual galaxies photo-z estimation. This effect is particularly harmful for the self-calibration method, since it has high requirements for reliable estimation of the photo-$z$s, and the need for individual galaxy point estimates and tomographic binning to match. We show how different methods of recreating the redshift probability distribution can affect the detection of intrinsic alignment.

papers.title: Increasing the Precision of Surrogate Models for Weak Lensing Mass Maps with Flow Matching
papers.authors: Guangjian Li, Tomasz Kacprzak
papers.abstract: Weak gravitational lensing maps compactly encode the evolution of cosmic large-scale structure and are a key tool for cosmological analyses. Performing inference directly at the map level allows flexible choices of statistics and can increase constraining power. Conventional methods rely solely on N-body simulations and are computationally expensive. Generative machine-learning emulators can accelerate map-level theory prediction. However, existing GAN-based map-level surrogates still have limited statistical fidelity. They can produce over-smoothed maps, may fail to capture the full distribution of generated map sets and can be difficult to train. Continuous normalizing flows trained with flow matching have recently emerged as a powerful class of generative models. We present a residual label-conditional flow matching generative network that conditions explicitly on the matter density $\Omega_m$ and clustering amplitude $\sigma_8$ for a fixed source redshift distribution $n(z)$. The model learns a continuous probability flow in a residual space from label-specific noise distributions to convergence maps. We evaluate it using pixel and peak statistics, the power spectrum, bispectrum, power-spectrum correlation matrices, and other validation metrics. Compared with the previous GAN benchmark, the proposed method improves the typical fidelity of generated maps from below 10% and below 20% to below 1% and below 5% for basic and higher-order statistics, respectively. The agreement at the level of map distributions is also very good: maps generated from random noise match well the distribution of maps generated with N-body simulations from random initial conditions. This work brings us closer to a practical mass-map emulator that captures the cosmological signal while supporting multiple forms of data analysis.

papers.title: Pushing the Primordial Frontier: Exact Linear Solutions in Multifield Inflation
papers.authors: Javier Huenupi, Claudio Muñoz, Gonzalo A. Palma, Spyros Sypsas
papers.abstract: We present exact analytic solutions for the linear dynamics of a two-field inflationary system in which the primordial curvature perturbation $\zeta$ is coupled to an isocurvature perturbation $\sigma$ of entropy mass $\mu$. The solutions are valid for arbitrary values of $\mu$ and the dimensionless interaction strength $\lambda$. They therefore provide analytic control over the strong mixing regime in which $\zeta$ interacts with light isocurvature fields, commonly associated with rapid-turn inflation. As a first application, we derive the amplitude of the primordial power spectrum in closed form, obtaining an expression that interpolates between the weakly mixed, strongly mixed, light-field, and heavy-field regimes. These results open the way to analytic studies of multifield observables beyond the power spectrum, including non-Gaussianity, particle production, and loop corrections.

papers.title: The youth of the intracluster medium. I. A non-parametric characterisation of the gas and electron number density profiles of $z \simeq 2$ protoclusters
papers.authors: David Vallés-Pérez, Annalisa Bonafede, Klaus Dolag, Marco Balboni, Paolo Tozzi, Marika Lepore
papers.abstract: Context. Protoclusters of galaxies are the earliest phase in the assembly of galaxy clusters and can provide invaluable information about plasma physics, cosmic magnetism, and cosmology. However, due to small angular sizes and cosmological dimming, observing the proto-intracluster medium (proto-ICM) associated with protocluster cores is far from trivial. Aims. We aim to provide a non-parametric description of the gas mass and electron number density profiles of the proto-ICM at $z = 2$, and to study their dependence on mass, dynamical state and central activity. Methods. We extract and analyse over $3800$ regions around protocluster cores with spherical-overdensity masses above $M_\mathrm{500c} > 10^{13} \, M_\odot$ out of a large simulated volume within the Magneticum suite. We study their density profiles, temperature structure, ionisation degree and electron number density as a function of mass and other secondary properties characterising dynamical state and central activity, extending from the central halo to the surrounding protocluster environment. Results. Protoclusters present moderate deviations from self-similarity in their density profiles and temperature structure, with a strong double-$\beta$ structure especially relevant at high masses and intense AGN accretion. Hot, ionised gas is only dominant at intermediate radii ($r \gtrsim [0.1-0.5] R_\mathrm{500c}$), where its density also correlates with mass and dynamical disturbance. Conclusions. These results constitute the basis for a forthcoming parametric calibration of proto-ICM density profiles, which could be useful for interpreting observables sensitive to the density and ionisation of the diffuse gas.

papers.title: Relativistic Chiral MHD with application to the early Universe
papers.authors: Deepen Lark, Jennifer Schober
papers.abstract: We present a systematic derivation of the equations of relativistic chiral magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) for a plasma of charged fermions in an expanding universe. Through a combination of a coordinate transformation and a rescaling of the dynamical variables, we bring the full system to the same form as in the Minkowski metric, with the Hubble expansion surviving only in the chirality-flipping rate and the kinematic viscosity. Retaining all four contributions to both the electric and the axial current yields terms absent from standard chiral MHD: charge-density corrections to the evolution equations for the chemical potentials, and an electric current proportional to the charge chemical potential $\mu$ and the bulk velocity. The latter is mandated by current conservation, requires no chirality imbalance, and drives the charge-flow instability studied in a follow-up paper. For the radiation-dominated era, we evaluate all the coefficients in physical units and use them to estimate the magnetic Reynolds number, the attainable magnetic field strength, and the minimum temperature at which the chiral dynamo can operate. The resulting equations are cast in a form ready for direct numerical implementation.

papers.title: EFT-Ramses: a code to simulate the effective field theory of dark energy
papers.authors: Nathaniel Ota Woodcock, Sownak Bose, Yunhao Gao, Baojiu Li
papers.abstract: While the standard $\Lambda$CDM paradigm is in excellent agreement with most current cosmological observations, theoretical challenges surrounding the cosmological constant ($\Lambda$) have strongly motivated the exploration of dynamical dark energy (DE) and modified gravity (MG) models. Investigating the physical nature of the cosmic acceleration requires N-body simulations to probe the non-linear growth of cosmic structure and prepare for the high-precision data from Stage-IV surveys. In this paper, we present EFT-RAMSES, a comprehensive extension of the ECOSMOG cosmological simulation code designed to explore non-linear structure formation in DE and MG scenarios. We embed the effective field theory of dark energy (EFTofDE) framework into this new numerical pipeline, utilising the $\alpha$-basis parameterisation to provide a versatile, model-agnostic, computational engine. By consolidating diverse scalar and vector-tensor theories---including the normal and self-accelerating Dvali-Gabadadze-Porrati (DGP) models, cubic Galileons (cubic scalar Galileon (csG), cubic vector Galileon (cvG) and generalised cubic covariant Galileon (GCCG)), and generic effective field theory (EFT) parameterisation---into a single "master" Vainshtein equation, this pipeline bypasses the need for model-specific solvers and easily specialises to any particular model. As validations, we perform high-resolution N-body simulations for the normal-branch DGP (nDGP), csG, GCCG, and EFT models, comparing the resulting matter power spectra against dependent and independent codes such as legacy ECOSMOG and HiCOLA, as well as linear theory, and find excellent agreement. EFT-RAMSES provides a robust and versatile computational tool for precision cosmological tests of DE and MG using upcoming cosmological surveys. The code is available for download from the GitHub EFT-RAMSES repository.

papers.title: AGN Reverberation Mapping with LITMUS: Fundamental Limits on lag Recovery Rates
papers.authors: Hugh McDougall, Tamara M. Davis, Benjamin J. S. Pope, Paul Martini, Zhefu Yu, Chris Lidman, Geraint F. Lewis
papers.abstract: Reverberation mapping of active galactic nuclei provides one of the most direct probes of the geometry and kinematics of the broad-line region by measuring time delays between continuum and line variability. Modern RM surveys frequently suffer difficulties with lag measurements due to poor signal to noise and aliasing, whereby multimodal lag posterior distributions arise due to seasonal gaps in our data. These challenge the reliability of commonly used fitting tools such as JAVELIN, which can return a high rate of false positives. We implement a new lag measurement package, LITMUS, and introduce a new framework that uses Bayesian evidence to identify false positive lag measurements, as well as examine the question of how many AGN present detectable lags in high redshift industrial scale surveys like OzDES and SDSS. Our analysis differs from previous RM studies in six key respects: (i) our inference is robust to the previously under-diagnosed numerical component of aliasing, (ii) we use a consistent methodology for all sources, (iii) uncertainty in the underlying AGN variability is fully marginalised, (iv) lag significance is assessed via Bayesian model comparison rather than heuristic metrics, (v) false-positive rates are quantified by comparison against random-chance recoveries and (vi) we use marginal likelihoods to distinguish between sources where a lag is not detectable in our data and sources that show no evidence of reverberation. Applied to the OzDES sample, we find that previous RM studies are likely to have overestimated the confidence of recovered lags, and we find a stark contrast between a low reverberation percentage for the MgII line (3-28% depending on assumptions) and much higher percentages in the CIV and especially the H$\beta$ line, which is consistent with 100%. We also present a re-analysed set of lags from the OzDES sample with better quantified reliabilities

papers.title: Limited Impact of CMB B-mode Polarization on Constraints on Cosmic Topology
papers.authors: Ryota Himeno, Atsushi J. Nishizawa, Kiyotomo Ichiki
papers.abstract: The global spatial structure of the universe is a fundamental question in cosmology. Although the standard model usually assumes a trivial topology, a multiply connected universe can break statistical isotropy and generate off-diagonal covariance between the spherical-harmonic coefficients of cosmic microwave background fluctuations. In this work, we investigate whether CMB B-mode polarization improves constraints on the cubic three-torus, or $E_1$ topology. We construct the full harmonic-space covariance matrices of the temperature, E-mode, and primordial B-mode anisotropies, including correlations between different $(\ell,m)$ modes, and evaluate Gaussian likelihoods using random realizations generated from a statistically isotropic $\Lambda$CDM model with trivial topology. To isolate the intrinsic topological information carried by each CMB observable, we consider the ideal cosmic-variance-limited case, neglecting instrumental noise and gravitational lensing. We find that adding primordial B-mode polarization yields only a marginal improvement in the ability to distinguish the $E_1$ topology from the trivial topology, even under these ideal conditions. The different constraining powers of the temperature, E-mode, and B-mode anisotropies can be understood through the combined effects of their transfer-function responses and the topology-induced off-diagonal correlations in harmonic space. }

papers.title: Correlations between Dynamical Dark Energy and Neutrino Parameters
papers.authors: Ching-Yu Leung, WangZheng Zhang, Ming-Chung Chu
papers.abstract: Recent Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), fitted jointly with Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) and Type Ia Supernovae (SNe) data, favor dynamical dark energy (DDE) over the standard $\Lambda$CDM model. In this work, we investigate whether the mass and degeneracy of relic neutrinos are degenerate with DDE parameters and can also account for this statistical deviation from $\Lambda$CDM. Using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analysis of a joint Planck CMB temperature, DESI BAO, and Pantheon+ dataset, we show a robust parameter degeneracy between the DDE equation of state and neutrino physics. We supplement this with a semi-analytical framework that recovers the numerical correlation, showing that the tight constraint on the CMB acoustic scale drives this degeneracy. Our results highlight the clear correlation between DDE and neutrino parameters, underscoring the critical need to jointly constrain the neutrino sector and the dark sector in next-generation cosmological surveys.

papers.title: Classical and Semiclassical Stability of Emergent Universes in Jordan-Brans-Dicke Theory
papers.authors: Pedro Labraña, Juan Ortiz
papers.abstract: The Emergent Universe scenario is based on the assumption that the universe originates from a past-eternal Einstein static (ES) state, subsequently evolving toward an inflationary phase and a hot Big Bang era. Such models are appealing as they provide nonsingular and geodesically complete cosmological histories. However, it has been argued by Mithani and Vilenkin that, even when the ES state is classically stable, certain models can admit semiclassical tunneling channels leading to quantum decay toward configurations of vanishing scale factor. In this work, we investigate the classical and semiclassical stability of the ES regime in the context of Jordan-Brans-Dicke (JBD) theory. We analyze the structure of the Wheeler-DeWitt potential in minisuperspace and study representative semiclassical tunneling channels compatible with the Hamiltonian constraint. We show that, for suitable choices of the JBD potential and model parameters, the ES configuration can be robust against both classical perturbations and the specific semiclassical tunneling channels analyzed in this work. Our results indicate that the quantum instability discussed by Mithani and Vilenkin may be avoided within certain regions of parameter space, while leaving open the possibility of more general tunneling processes beyond the scope of the present analysis.

papers.title: Intrinsically Quantum Effects of Axion Dark Matter are Undetectable
papers.authors: Yunjia Bao, Dhong Yeon Cheong, Nicholas L. Rodd, Joey Takach, Lian-Tao Wang, Kevin Zhou
papers.abstract: Is the usual treatment of axion dark matter as a classical field reliable? We show that the answer is subtle: the axion field could well be in a quantum state that has no complete classical description, but realistic detectors cannot tell the difference. To see this, we solve a fully quantum model of axion detection using quantum optics techniques. We show that intrinsically quantum effects are washed out by mode averaging or small amounts of noise, and significantly suppressed by the weakness of the axion coupling. Our work exemplifies that there should always be a classical analog for axion dark matter effects, extends to other wave (ultralight) dark-matter candidates, and gives a general method to compute the effects of exotic dark-matter states.

papers.title: The Evolution of the Spin Alignments of Dark Matter Halos in the Cosmic Web
papers.authors: David Tobar, Rory Smith, Antonio Montero-Dorta, Katarina Kraljic, Pablo López
papers.abstract: We investigate the evolution of dark matter halo spin alignments with respect to cosmic filaments, exploring how halo mass, proximity to filaments, and major mergers influence their orientation over time. We perform a suite of dark matter-only zoom-in N-body simulations centered on ten filaments extracted from a cosmological box using the 1DREAM structure finder. This approach allows us to resolve low-mass halos within filaments while preserving the large-scale environment. Halos are identified with the Amiga Halo Finder (AHF), and their evolutionary histories are reconstructed to trace the spin, shape, and distance to the filament from redshift $z = 1$ to $z = 0$. We confirm a strong mass-dependent alignment signal: low-mass halos tend to align parallel to the filament, while high-mass halos preferentially exhibit perpendicular orientations, despite limited statistics. Perpendicular alignments become dominant at the highest halo masses in our sample, around $\log_{10}(M_\mathrm{h}/h^{-1}\mathrm{M_\odot}) \sim 12$. We also find that major mergers can induce sharp spin reorientations and temporary transitions toward more prolate halo shapes, particularly in massive halos located near the filament core, suggesting a preferential merger direction within filaments. Overall, halo mass emerges as the primary factor governing spin-filament alignments in our sample. By analyzing the global evolution, we find that the average orientations at z = 0 do not differ significantly from those at $z = 1$, indicating that the present-day spin configuration is largely established at earlier stages of halo evolution. Major mergers, although relatively rare, represent one of the few mechanisms capable of disrupting this initial alignment.

papers.title: Flavomons in Matter Gradients: Ray Tracing and Amplitude Evolution
papers.authors: Damiano F. G. Fiorillo, Georg G. Raffelt
papers.abstract: Flavor instabilities develop in neutrino plasmas through the emission of flavomons, collective excitations of the flavor field. Matter gradients can sweep flavomons across the unstable wave-number range, halting their amplification. This effect is parametrically small for fast modes, where it was first identified, but we show that it strongly alters neutrino-mass-induced instabilities below the supernova shock, while leaving those outside largely unaffected. Dispersion relations alone, which are inevitably local, cannot determine the cumulative amplification of slow instabilities. Using the WKB approximation, we derive the covariant evolution equation for the flavomon amplitude along geometrical-optics rays, enabling a global treatment of instability growth and seeding.

papers.title: Minimum lifetime of a black hole
papers.authors: Eugenio Bianchi, Matthew Brandsema, Kenneth Czuprynski, Daniel E. Paraizo
papers.abstract: We derive bounds on the lifetime of an evaporating black hole. The minimum lifetime bound follows from energy conservation and purification, within the framework of `asymptotically semiclassical spacetimes'. The recently derived expression for the Bondi flux of Hawking radiation, together with the expression for the entanglement entropy of Hawking radiation at null infinity, is used to investigate the purification phase after the last semiclassical ray. We discuss the energy-cost of entanglement purification and find a lower bound on the purification time of the black hole, which scales as $M_0^4/\hbar^{3/2}$, where $M_0$ is the initial black hole mass. Additionally, motivated by the Planck luminosity bound in quantum gravity, we include the additional assumption that a Planck mass black hole is metastable. With this assumption, the purification time is in fact exponential in the square of the initial black hole mass, $\tau\sim\sqrt{\hbar}\,\exp(\gamma M_0^2/\hbar)$ with $\gamma>0$, i.e., exponential in its initial area. We find that the redshift exponent is negative in this purification phase, which indicates the existence of a white-hole remnant that releases information slowly. We comment on phenomenological implications for primordial black hole remnants.

papers.title: Probing the dynamical inverse seesaw mechanism with low-frequency gravitational waves
papers.authors: Debasish Borah, Sounak Dutta, Partha Kumar Paul, Indrajit Saha, Narendra Sahu
papers.abstract: We study the possibility of probing the dynamical inverse seesaw mechanism for the origin of light neutrino masses via the detection of stochastic gravitational waves (GW) in the low-frequency regime currently being probed by pulsar timing arrays. As the lepton number-violating term in inverse seesaw typically remains in the sub-MeV ballpark, its dynamical origin naturally brings the possibility of a low-scale first-order phase transition, which can be probed at low-frequency GW experiments. We also find interesting complementarity with heavy neutral lepton searches, as GW experiments remain sensitive to parameter space with small active-sterile mixing, which is out of reach for most particle physics experiments.

papers.title: sft-wick: A formalism and package for Feynman-diagram expansion and evaluation in stochastic field theories
papers.authors: Zheng Zhang
papers.abstract: When stochastic field dynamics are cast into a path-integral formulation, perturbation theory becomes systematic but the resulting expansion quickly grows combinatorially large. The setting targeted here includes fields with several components and several dimensions, matrix propagators, tensor-valued couplings, and non-Gaussian driving noise specified by arbitrary n-point cumulants. Wick pairings grow factorially, and component indices must be routed through the tensor-valued vertices. The useful output is not a raw contraction list, but a diagram table: one entry per topology, with multiplicities, coupling sums, signs, and causal constraints resolved. We present sft-wick, an open-source Python package that constructs these diagram tables and computes their integrals numerically. Given an action and an observable, it enumerates topologically distinct Feynman diagrams, derives their algebraic coefficients, and evaluates the resulting diagram integrals from user-supplied response and cumulant functions. The core algorithm enumerates spatial topologies before routing component indices, avoiding contraction-by-contraction Wick expansion. Response-field constraints, including vanishing response-response contractions, the Ito prescription, and the absence of causal response loops, are enforced during enumeration. Predictions are validated against direct Langevin simulations in two worked examples, with Gaussian and with non-Gaussian driving noise, and agree with the simulations within stated error budgets.

papers.title: Background-Induced Forces from Quadratically Coupled Ultralight Dark Matter
papers.authors: Thomas Bouley, Xucheng Gan, Hailin Xu, Tien-Tien Yu
papers.abstract: Quadratically coupled ultralight scalar dark matter behaves as a coherent classical field whose interactions with matter can induce a composition-dependent force through the dark matter background. We present a complete calculation of this background-induced force beyond the spherically symmetric approximation. Using a partial-wave treatment of dark-matter scattering, we determine its angular dependence and derive an analytic description valid even when the dark-matter wavelength is much smaller than the Earth's radius. We show for the first time that Earth screening generates a characteristic frequency-band structure, splitting the signal into multiple sidebands that provide a distinctive experimental signature. We further show that the relative amplitudes of these sidebands vary annually as the satellite's Sun-synchronous orbital plane precesses in step with the Earth's revolution around the Sun, allowing us to construct a complete signal template. As an application of these results, we re-evaluate constraints from the MICROSCOPE mission, which currently provides the strongest laboratory limits on equivalence-principle violations from ultralight dark matter. We further show that proposed space-based equivalence-principle experiments, such as Galileo Galilei and STE-QUEST, can significantly enhance their sensitivity to ultralight scalar dark matter by incorporating the full frequency-band information.

papers.title: Corrections to Hawking radiation from asteroid-mass primordial black holes: analytic and numerical evaluation of the stochastic charge effect
papers.authors: Gabriel Vasquez, Bowen Chen, Cara Nel, Emily Koivu, Makana Silva, Christopher M. Hirata
papers.abstract: Hawking radiation sets stringent constraints on Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) as a dark matter candidate in the $M\sim 10^{16}$ g regime based on the evaporation products produced by the black hole, motivating the need to rigorously model the photon, electron, and positron emission spectra. This manuscript is the second in a series of two papers (see Vasquez et al. [Phys. Rev. D, 112:063002 (2025)] for the first paper in the series) with the goal of proving the stochastic emission of electrons and positrons, known as the "stochastic charge effect" and first predicted by Page [Phys. Rev. D, 16:2402 (1977)] using semi-classical arguments, arises from quantum electrodynamics (QED) on a Schwarzschild spacetime. We derive the corrections to the $e^\pm$ from the relevant term in the Hamiltonian (the long-range monopole: $H_{\rm int,0L}$) to first order in the fine structure constant ($\alpha$), and show that the semi-classical terms are also present in the QED calculation. We also highlight which terms in our analysis only appear within our quantum mechanical approach and cannot be explained otherwise. We find that due to some cancellation of terms, over the range of $2.2\times 10^{16}$ - $1.7\times 10^{17}$ g, the net correction to the $e^\pm$ emission rate is less than 2%, versus the suppression of up to 5% previously found by semi-classical arguments.

papers.title: The alternative scalar field dark sector of the Universe: Cosmological inflation, quintessence and ekpyrotic model in the framework of scalar-tensor cosmology
papers.authors: Marcin Postolak
papers.abstract: This dissertation investigates scalar field descriptions of the dark sector (of the Universe), with emphasis on scalar-tensor cosmology, inflationary effective field theory, quintessence, and ekpyrotic/cyclic alternatives to inflation. The thesis first reviews scalar-tensor theories of gravity, starting from Brans-Dicke theory and extending to general non-minimally coupled scalar fields. Particular attention is paid to the interpretation of the scalar field, the relation between the Jordan and Einstein conformal frames, and the role of conformal transformations in cosmology. This provides the theoretical basis for treating scalar fields either as modified matter or as additional gravitational degrees of freedom. The second part discusses cosmological inflation from the viewpoint of effective field theory. The spontaneous breaking of time translations, the Goldstone description of adiabatic perturbations, higher-dimensional operators, radiative corrections and Planck-suppressed terms are analyzed in the context of ultraviolet sensitivity and the eta problem. The third part is devoted to quintessence as the simplest dynamical dark energy model. 'Tracking', 'scaling', 'thawing' and 'freezing' behaviors are discussed, together with observational diagnostics such as the statefinder parameters, the $(\omega_{\phi},\omega'_{\phi})$ plane and the $Om(z)$ diagnostic. The DESI DR2 results are used as motivation for considering time-dependent effective dark energy beyond a strict cosmological constant. The final part studies ekpyrotic and cyclic cosmologies. The ekpyrotic phase is analyzed as a smoothing mechanism based on an ultra-stiff scalar field equation of state. Perturbations, non-Gaussianity, tensor modes, bounce conditions, entropy production, geodesic incompleteness and phase-resolved field-space distance bounds are discussed.

papers.abstract: The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory will complete its ten-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) in the mid-2030s. Its 8.4 m aperture and 9.6 square degree field of view give it an étendue unmatched by any facility planned for that era. The Rubin 2036: Opportunities for Discovery workshop (KIPAC/SLAC, 3-5 August 2026) brought together approximately 100 participants to discuss Rubin's future after LSST. This paper summarizes the workshop's structure and discussions across five working groups. The continued-surveying group explored a machine-learning foundation model pretrained on Rubin imaging for detection, deblending, and classification. The cadence group considered allocating post-LSST observing time and strategies for transiting exoplanets, Type Ia supernova cosmology, time-delay cosmography, and second-scale transients. The filter group explored broadband, medium-band, and narrowband filters for photometric redshifts, high-redshift large-scale structure, AGN reverberation mapping, Galactic archaeology, and emission-line imaging. The multi-messenger group explored follow-up of next-generation gravitational-wave and neutrino sources, including standard sirens, kilonovae, and Galactic supernovae. The technology group organized options by cost and lead time, including fast readout, new filters, a faster shutter, and summit edge computing. Cross-cutting topics included AI/ML, Chilean and Latin-American co-leadership, satellite megaconstellations, and weather and climate trends at Cerro Pachón.
